'''Peter Meyer''' (January 6, 1920 – March 7, 2002) was a German-born American [[astrophysicist]] notable for his research of [[cosmic rays]].<ref name="LA-TIMES">{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2002-mar-11-me-passings11.3-story.html|title=Peter Meyer, 82; Physicist Studied Cosmic Rays|first=L. A. Times|last=Archives|date=March 11, 2002|website=Los Angeles Times}}</ref><ref name="UCHICAGO">{{Cite web|url=http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/020411/obit-meyer.shtml|title=Physicist Meyer dies at age 82|website=chronicle.uchicago.edu}}</ref><ref name="NAP">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/publications/biographical-memoirs/|title=Biographical Memoirs - NAS|website=nasonline.org}}</ref><ref name="AAS">{{Cite web|url=https://baas.aas.org/pub/peter-meyer-1920-2002/release/1 |title=Obituary: Peter Meyer, 1920-2002 |last=Müller |first=D.
|journal=Bulletin of the American Astronomical Society |volume=34 |issue= 4 |pages=1368-1370}}</ref> 
Meyer was director of the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] at the [[University of Chicago]],<ref name="LA-TIMES"/> was a chairman of the [[University of Chicago]]'s physics department,<ref name="LA-TIMES"/>
and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="NAP"/>
He was also chair of the Cosmic Ray Physics Division of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref name="NAP"/> a member of the Space Science Board of the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name="NAP"/> and chair of the Committee on Astronomy and Astrophysics of the Space Science Board.<ref name="NAP"/>

== Biography ==
Meyer was born in [[Berlin, Germany]], in a Jewish family. He studied at the [[Technical University in Berlin]], where he received [[Engineering degree|Diplom Ingenieur]] (1942), with a thesis on proportional counters. He was not permitted to study on a PhD level in Germany as a Jew, and worked in a factory during the war.<ref name="AAS"/> He received a doctorate from the [[University of Göttingen]] in 1948, with [[Wolfgang Paul]] and [[Hans Kopfermann]] as advisers.<ref name="AAS"/><ref name="NAP"/> He then had a postdoc position in the [[Cavendish Laboratory]], and then worked as a researcher in the Max Planck Institute for Physics at Göttingen.<ref name="AAS"/>

He immigrated to the United States in 1953 and joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]], where he worked with [[John A. Simpson]].<ref name="AAS"/> Meyer advanced to assistant professor in 1956, associate professor in 1962 and professor in 1966. He was the Director of the Enrico Fermi Institute from 1978 to 1983. Meyer spent the rest of his career at the University of Chicago and became emeritus in 1990.<ref name="AAS"/> He received the [[Quantrell Award]].<ref name="Prize">{{cite web|title=Llewellyn John and Harriet Manchester Quantrell Awards for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching|url=https://www.uchicago.edu/who-we-are/global-impact/accolades/llewellyn-john-and-harriet-manchester-quantrell-awards-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-teaching|website=UChicago}}</ref>

Meyer experimented with balloon-borne cosmic ray detectors; together with Simpson he built one of the first instruments for cosmic ray experiments flown on spacecraft.<ref name="AAS"/>

Meyer was "an accomplished cellist", who often played with his first wife. He was married twice, to physicist [[Luise Meyer-Schützmeister]] (d. 1981), and to virologist [[Patricia G. Spear]]. He had two sons.<ref name="AAS"/>

Meyer died in Chicago from complications of a stroke.<ref name="AAS"/> His doctoral students include [[Rochus E. Vogt]].<ref name="AAS"/>
